blocks.x: I got it from him last year.

My Godfather used to be a great undertaker on Ramport and... Well, this street here... Well, they changed the two names. No. Governor Nichols. Governor Nichols. He gave me his name. Floreston is my first name. R-Font is the second one. Piku, well that's the family. You see? But I changed that Floreston because I had so much trouble with Piku, you know? Yeah. For the pronunciation. So I said, well make it Alphonse. You see? Yeah.

To the radio.

Smith. Macy or Mamie? Macy or Mamie? Macy Smith.

There where the jazz can be.

Yeah. George Bacchia. Yeah. George Bacchia. Yes. Lorenzo Tio and George Bacchia. We were the only three clarinet players in your league.
You know? Yeah.

Yeah.
I see.

I don't like that.

Did you ever play the Bame System Clarinet or always the Albert? Oh, yeah. I played both of them. You played both of them? Yeah. But already Albert. Why do you like the Albert better? Yeah, because Albert for jazz is more easy than the band. Because the band has got too much keys. And the Albert, he got less keys than the band. That's why I'm mad.
Do you think there's any difference in the tone? Albert. Albert. Do you think there's any difference in the tone? No. No difference in the tone? No difference in the tone. No difference in the tone.

That's nice. E flat.

Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Somebody started somewhere.
Yeah. Somebody started somewhere.

Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah.

Yeah. Yeah. When did you first hear the blues? Did you, when you were a boy, did they sing the blues or play the blues on the instruments? When you were a boy learning on guitar? I was the first man that composed the blues. I used to play by Billy Phillips on Zero and Aberdeen. Now, I'll tell you how I learned the blues. Me and my friend, Jimmy Brown, that used to be in our band, and he used to be the bass player. So he had a woman that used to come on the piano. We had a piano. So one day he told me, say, Pike, I want you to come with me. I said, where? Come on. I went with him on the railroad on the front by the river. And that time, he was putting up a track. You know? And they had one band that was singing the blues. You know? I said, Pike, listen right there. I said, see, they sound good at you. The blues, he was singing the blues. I said, listen. He said, could you do something with that? I said, sure. I said, I got that back down. He says to me, well, I'll tell you. I said, do you know the words of, oh, he said, I got that. Oh, so we got everything. So I went at my house. We're here. I took my piano. And I blow that melody for him. And then he said, and that night, we went, because we had a steady job, you know, for a life. And that night, we put it on. There's where the blues comes from. Who's coming from? First time. That was in the district then. In the district. That was the district.
How old were you when you got married now, Paul?
Right, K2.
Uh-huh.
That's where I started smelling myself.
Where you started?

Smelling myself. Smelling myself. Smelling myself. You know? You're just getting to their heart. Oh, you know that. You must have been crying. Oh, you know that. You know that. You know that. You know that. Because you're a young man. You know that. And during the time you were married, during that time,
you were working in the district for a long time. Oh, yes, indeed. I used to work in the district.

Where we used to go at eight o'clock. And play from eight to four. How about you think? Dollar and a quarter a night. Wow. You know that's like a thing. Dollar and a quarter a night. Was that like in a night club? Yeah. Uh-huh. Yeah. I forgot his name.
Did people dance there? No, not much dance.
Not much dance. Not much dance. Not much dance.
But ask for the numbers that they want. Yeah. We had to play them.
Yeah, do you remember the numbers they used to ask for? No. None of them, huh? Just popular songs or... Yeah, old songs. The old songs. Yeah, old songs. Yeah, old songs.
Yeah, old songs. Yeah, old songs. Yeah, old songs. Yeah, old songs.
Yeah, old songs. But you don't remember the names of those songs, huh? No, no. I don't know.

Customers come in and have a drink?
Customers. Customers. Uh-huh. Now, the customers used to come from the... Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh.

Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. They come away. And it's all white. Yeah. And they come from away. They will ask us the player number. The fellow will come with a $10 bill, give you that, just like he'd give you a liquor. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. But with half a dollar and a quarter. You understand? Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Remember that number? We never did forget that. How many people were in the band to split that up? How many? Four. Four. Four. What did you have? The guitar and bass? Or did you use the piano? Sometimes the piano.
The piano, you should play guitar, you know? Tell me, Alfonso, what did you do when you were playing those jobs, such long hours, when you got hungry? Why did you do it for food?
Oh, we used to have a little restaurant on Bass Street. And you know what was my meal? Or No. 7 state. That was bar food.
Number 7?
Number 7.
Number 7 state.
Number 7 state. That was bar food.
What was that? Is that the biggest one they had? The biggest one they had? Yeah. Number 7. Did all the musicians go to the same place?

Same place. Uh-huh. Is that Turo's or? Huh? Is that Turo? Or? No, Bassin and the man that ran there. Huh? The man that had that restaurant. He was on the Biscine. Oh yeah, on Bassin and, uh, Bassin and Aberville. Or Biemble. Or Biemble. I think Biemble. I forgot the name of the restaurant. I thought it was Turo. Did Manuel Mineta tell us about the restaurant? Yeah. Manuel Mineta would play with me on Biemble. Yeah. I was, I was, I was, we used to play ticket. How about transportation? How did you used to get back and forth from work? Huh? How did you get back and forth from work? Well, you could walk to work, couldn't you? Oh yeah. That's right. It wasn't very far. Second, second walk. Yeah. We did worry about that. Uh-huh.
Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh.
Uh-huh. Uh-huh.

Lula White. Uh-huh. Lula White. I thought about pretty woman, can you show? Lula White. Yeah, look like I'm looking at her. Hey, you all making me think about anything else like that. Lula White. Ice and snow?
Yeah.

I see.

Can you tell us anything about the real French Opera? Did you ever go to the French Opera when you were a boy and see the opera? I used to be crazy about the French Opera. I used to love, not like, love the eggs. The French. Oh, yeah, because my father, Frenchman. Yes. Oh, no. I used to live right one block from the French Opera. On St. Peter? St. Peter? Boybock. St. Peter? Boybock. Yes. One block I had to walk. And I had to go that high step, you know? Fifteen cents. Oh, yeah, that's fifteen cents up in the balcony. Yeah. You know I ain't lying. No, I'm sorry. No, I'm sorry. Yes, sir. What? I love French. That's a language I love and Spanish. I love them two languages. Do you speak Spanish too?
See?
Spanish? Do you speak Spanish too?
Yeah. Oh. Do you speak Spanish?
You speak Spanish? Bastante?
Yes. Oh. Do you speak Spanish? Bastante? Yes. Bastante? Yes. Mucho gracias, señor. That means a little bit. Speak a little bit in Spanish.

Es lo mismo.

Let's talk a little talk. Yeah. Tell me, did you, in those days, ever play any band concerts? Yes. They had band concerts in the park and so on. Did you play in those? Yes. Were they the same musicians who played in the band concerts as played in the music? No.

I can take that instrument, I can go in the jazz band, I can go in any band, I can go to the French opera and play with any band, so long they put it in front of me. As long as the music's up there, you can. Just put it in front of me and I got you. Is your clarinet the same, fingering is the same keys as your drum? Yeah, yeah. Same thing you got.

Oh shit. Oh.

Oh dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear

Countries.

Do you remember who was in the band? Mm-hm.

Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Charlie Booker. This man, as long as he lives, he'll play as well as he ever did. He said, you send for Mr. Peek Coot. That's it. That's it. That's it. You said the right thing. All of them.

Alexander.

And there is another band, George Moret. Or Moret, how do you pronounce it?
Moret. Yes. That was his first band, wasn't it?
One of the best sharp play we had in New Orleans. He used to hit a high note in a parade because he had way up above. He was Carlos Tower. Talk about that? Yes, indeed.
Is that the same George Moret who hired you off Governor Nichol Street for your first job?

Yes. Yes. And another man, Oscar Duconge, D-U-C-O-N-G-E is the way I have his spell. Duconge? Duconge. Duconge. Yes. Duconge. Yes. What kind of a band did he have? Well, he had a good affair band. What did he play? Duconge used to play, let me see, I can't remember that. Cornet. Cornet. The brass band wasn't it? Yes. When you had your own band, when you were the leader, what name did you call that? If you were the leader of the band, when did you, in the old days, did you have a name for the band? No, I know. Are you just... Yes. Like say, for instance, some of them had the imperial band, and that was Manuel Perez's band, wasn't it? The imperial band. Yes. Did you ever have a band of your own that you were the leader that you would give it any certain name? Yes. Let me see if I can remember that name. The Golden Leaf. Golden Leaf. Golden Leaf. Golden Leaf. Oh my God. It was your band. Was there a band called the Independent Band? Yes. That was your band too, Independent. Yes, that was the first band I played in. That was the first one. Yes. Bubu Fortune, like I was telling you. Yes. What was his last name? Bubu Fortune. Fortuny. Fortuny. Fortuny. He was a Bob. He was a fellow about that high. Looked like a Mexican. Yes.
Well, if you were talking to a young fellow now that was getting ready to be a professional musician, is there any special advice that you would give him?
Oh, yes.
What would you tell him? What would you tell Ralph here about?

How you blow it, that's all. The right way to blow it. In other words, to learn his horn. Yes, that's the first one. What I would like to do with some of this material that you are recording, I would like to, if possible, get some of it published someday. If you had any advice to give about playing like in a jazz band, just what you do with a tune, so that young musicians that are coming up and will come up in future years would have an idea just what your advice would be. If you are going to play any kind of a late popular tune, just any kind of a tune, what do you try to do when you make up your clarinet part? Well, I'll tell you how we used to do it. We had our band and they asked us to play a waltz. All right. We played that waltz in a waltz time. And then we change it to jazz time. That's it. Jazz time. When you play it in jazz time, do you try to play more notes or what do you do to change the melody? How do you change it? How do you change it? Aside from changing the time, I know you change the time. Well, it's to change the time, that's all. Otherwise you...

As a clarinet player, do you find that you yourself prefer to play more melody or harmony? That is, do you leave the melody to the trumpet player and play the clarinet harmony part or do you have a tendency to sometimes want to play the melody itself in the ensemble?

I've wondered about the variations that you make if you try to just play a lot of chords, or if you'd rather play sort of a counter melody sometime, what do you think sounds best on the clarinet? Well, that depends what they got in you about variations.
Do you usually find that you like to practice your clarinet part or do you like to wait until the band is playing and then figure it out while they're playing?
Figure out while they're playing.
Mm-hmm.
Why they play?
It always comes out better that way. Yes, it comes right to you. You don't try to memorize things. No, no. It all comes to you.
It all comes to you.
Yeah.

Another question. In the old days, did they play many solos? Like nowadays, they'll play a piece, the whole orchestra, and then maybe the trumpet will play a solo, the clarinet will play a solo, the trombone will play a solo. In the old days, did you keep playing all the time or did they have a few solos mixed in too? Well, that depends what number you're playing.
Did you have trouble finding piano players to play the right chords?
Oh, yes.
I see. It was hard to find piano players always. Yes, it is. Yes, it is. And was it...
Especially now.
Yeah, but in the old days it was hard too. Yeah. Was it also hard to find drummers that could keep the beat?
Oh, drummers. We got no more.
Yes. But in the old days it was easy to find a drummer.

Who were some of the best drummers? You mentioned the old man Cantrell. Is that Cantrell or Cottrell? Do you remember? Cottrell. How is it? Cottrell. Cottrell. Yes. Now the best drummer we got is Paul Barbarelli. Yes, he's a drummer. That's the best one right now, on the drum. Yes. Yes. He was a drummer. He beat the last one. He got... Pudum, pum, pum, pum.
Who were the best of them before? Alfonso? Louis Cantrell. Louis Cantrell. And there were other ones as good? That was the king. He was the king.
He was the king.
Were there other good drummers around at that time? No.

Oh, yes. They had... Let me see, what's his name again? I just mentioned... Oh, dear. Oh, Lord. He used to play with us. Murray. Oh, yes. Charlie Murray. Charlie? Murray. Johnny. Johnny. Johnny Murray. Was that the brother of the other... No, Murray. Murray. Murray. Murray. Oh, I can't make sure. Was his name Murray or Mac Murray or... Yes, Mac Murray. Mac Murray. Murray, yes. Murray. Murray. That was another good drum. Did you know Happy Chandler? Happy was good, too. Is he good? Yes. We used to play together at the theatre. What? The Laird theatre. Robichaux. With John Robichaux. Yes.

Did they ever use any instruments that are not used anymore now, before? Now they usually just have a trumpet, trombone, and clarinet for horns. Occasionally saxophone. Were there other horns that were specialties of the old bands?
Did they ever use saxophone much in those days? No. No saxes in the old days.
They used melophone. They used melophone. Melophone.
And sousaphone.
Yeah. Susaphone. Did they ever use any instruments like bass trumpets or slide tubas? Yeah. They had all those things. Yeah.
What about violins when you were young? Oh, violins. That was the king.
They never played jazz on them, did they? Oh, yes.
Or just dancing.
Like P. Rau. Uh-huh.

Now, what kind of a part did the violin play? Something like the clarinet or the lead? No, the lead. They always played just the straight balloting? The lead. The lead. Yes. Did you like working with a violin in a band? Yes, it did. That's why it's so little. A band. For what I think played. Yes. I was wondering, when was the first time you heard Tiger Rag played by a dance band? Can you remember who was the first one to play it or when you heard it about? No, I don't.
Or Jack Carey? I don't remember.

I don't remember. I was going to ask a bit more about your clarinet. What make is your clarinet? Is it a... Algar. Algar system. I mean, is it made in France or... Yeah, I remember. Yeah, one is in France. You don't remember the maker of it now. Is it Buffet or who made it? It has that peculiar... Oh, no, I got that bar. I forgot that bar. That's a hard name for France. It's a hard French name. Yeah, French name.
Did anybody else use that curved bell that you have? No. You're the only one who has it here.
It's the only one I've ever seen.
Is that a standard instrument in France or is it one that you had made special? No.
It's standard from France.
In other words, in France they do you have...
The man that made the present, that clarinet, he was the... Oh, I keep getting... He was one of the hate men at the Werlein music place on Canal Street. Oh, Lord, what's his name?
Not Frank? Eh? Frank? Not Frank? No, he's got a French name.

No, he's got a French name. No, no. He's got a French name. Oh, Lord. It was a long time ago, though. Yes. About 30 years. A few things I was going to ask about. When you were a boy and started playing, how long did you practice when you first took up the instrument? Eight months. And how much each day did you... How long did you practice? I can't tell you that. I learned this morning. I can't tell you that. But I learned by instrument in eight months. In eight months you learned. Eight months. Did you practice every day? Oh, yes. A lot? Yes. How young do you think a clarinet player should start? How big should a boy be when he starts up? About sixteen. Wait until he's... Around sixteen or so. Not starting when he's ten or eight or nine, he's too young. No, no.
Do you think that it's a good idea to make children learn musical instruments or do you think it's better to wait until they want to learn?

Yes. That's the best. When they want to learn. When they want to learn. What a feeling is getting. That's right. Yes. We don't want to bother here. In another five minutes maybe we'll be through. I want to keep you all day. I know. I've got the time and I've got the money. All this is very important really. Thank you. We certainly enjoy hearing this. I feel that a lot of young students that want to learn clarinet would like to hear you talk too. I know that you and not many people have the opportunity to come and talk to you or to hear you play. It's hard to hear you play but at least if we can maybe publish some of this sometime and they'll be able to read your remarks and read your advice to students just what to do. See there's people all over the world who know who Kukou is. Oh yes. As you know they come here from Europe and England and France. They always want to meet you. One question I want to ask is that how long did you play with Papa, Paul Spaniel? About sixteen years. About sixteen years. About sixteen years. Long time. That was, was that at the time, no that wouldn't be at the time you were out in California were you? Yes. Did you go out in California with them? No. No. No. That was during that time you were playing with them. I was in California with a kid, kid old.
Do you remember Sidney Airding?
Oh.
Did he ever take any lessons from you? Who? Sidney Airding.
Oh sure.
I tell you.
Ah, the boss. They all come under these. How about Rapolo? Do you know Rapolo? Sure. Uh huh. I think he's probably studied with his father I think. Yeah. Yeah.

Now do you think it's possible to learn the clarinet just by yourself even without learning to read music? Like some people just pick it up. Sidney Bechet never did learn to read music so well I don't believe did he?

I don't think he reads much music but he plays wonderful I think. Sidney Bechet learned how to play the clarinet with a tin flute. What an tin flute. That's the way he learned. From that he pick up the clarinet. He used to come back to my house and I'll finish him up all the clarinet. Is it possible to learn to play pretty well without learning to read music very well do you think? Or do you advise people to learn music, to read the music first? Learn how to read music first. That's the first thing to do. Then you do it the right thing. Yes. When you started you had a regular method book. Oh yeah. Regular method book. You don't remember what book it was I guess. Yeah. Let me see what's the name of that book. Tell me.
Do you have a personal collection of things like music, sheet music and do you say photographs, records? What kind of things do you have that you own yourself now that have to do with jazz?
Well, I got a very nice income that's coming to me all the time.

No, I don't mean that, Alphonse. I mean do you have things like, do you have your own collection of music, do you have sheet music of your own? Oh yeah. And do you have, do you collect, do you save any old photographs?
Yes.

Do you have a lot of old pictures? Yes. Yes. And do you keep all that stuff together like in a book? All together, in a book. I see. Yes. And do you, would it be possible do you think sometime for us to look at them and see some of those?
I'll show you all, next time you'll come. I would like, we could stop by your home sometime. All right, do that. So you wouldn't have to bother to bring it here. I'll show you all everything.
It might be true that we would like very much that maybe to have an opportunity to copy some of that.
That's right. Sometime you can take an old photograph and then take a picture of that again and get a picture from the old. Okay, that's fine. That's nice.
We would like to see those. All right. I've got plenty of that. You don't have a picture of Tony Jackson, do you?
No. I had it, but I got it now. Okay, sure, tell me. Anything else you want to ask about Tony Jackson?
Well, I'm making an album on Tony Jackson myself, but there are a lot of questions that I'll ask you some other time about him. All right. Because...
I know what you want to ask me. Yeah. I know. You want that? I know. I know what you know too. We know that. All right.

Well, there are a lot of things that I would like to know. You don't happen to have any of the sheet music of his tunes, do you? No. Uh-huh. And do you have pictures of any of the old bands? Yes. Uh-huh. Here. That's something that I know Bill would be interested in.
Yes.
Yes, I'd like to see those sometime.

You'll see them. Next time you all come, I'll get them for them. I was hoping you would maybe play a little tune for us before we went out on. You went. I thought maybe you'd play us a little tune this morning, on Ukraine. Oh, yeah. It's Lanko. Oh, I know. Some other time. Some other time. Do you still play on Sunday evenings? Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Oh, maybe I'll come around here. Come on here. And you have it. About what time is the best time? Oh, we start at 8.30. Yes, sir?
One thing I wanted to ask too was this. Uh, is there anything that you have had in your mind that you would like to record, that you have never recorded, that you never had an opportunity to do?
Yes. Yes. Yes. What is that? Yes. I got four, I got four numbers by all composition. And I never had the opportunity of recording them.
Are they written down? Yes. Mm-hmm.
I tried it with Papa Celeste. Uh-huh. But I never did succeed yet. Uh-huh. I got one number. It's based on high society. Uh-huh. The variation with the clarinet and all that.
Nobody's had a chance to hear it, though. Uh-huh.

They tried it and that's all. They didn't like it. Too hard to learn, maybe. Yes, yes. Oh, yes, very hard. Maybe Bill could get you praying that sometimes. Why, you see? They got a gang of fellows here, come with it, give it up. You know? That's not the right type of a band to play those strings here. They have to be able to read all those. I say, can you all follow me? They say, hell no. Oh, no. I say, come on. Oh, God. No. No. Oh, God. No. Well, someday maybe you'll get to play those. You have them arranged for orchestra or just have the piano parts. How do you have it written out? Just with the piano and the clarinet or how? No, the whole band. The whole band. The whole band. The whole orchestration of it. Yes. Is there a hospital? No. We'd like to see those too sometime. In nice, sometimes, get a band together and play those. Yes. Are there any other pieces that you wrote that are played much? That's what I've thought about.
I mean, others that people do play.
Any other thing besides, like the high society, can you think of some others that you wrote?
Do you remember the titles of any of those?

Sure. I've got them all. No. One thing I was going to ask you Alfonso, is that you have written a lot of songs, and you have written a lot of songs. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. It should be good man. No no.

segments.title: Picou's name and his godfather
segments.summary: Picou explains his godfather, who was an undertaker, and how Floreston and Piku became Alphonse.

segments.title: When the word jazz was first heard
segments.summary: The interviewer asks when people first used the word jazz; Picou wanders to the first woman to sing the blues on radio.

segments.title: Early jazz bands and fellow clarinetists Tio and Baquet
segments.summary: Picou says he helped lead the move to jazz bands; Lorenzo Tio and George Baquet were the only three clarinetists of his standing, playing funerals together.

segments.title: Last time playing with Lorenzo Tio, and the Tio family
segments.summary: Picou recalls a party in Los Angeles where he last played with Tio, and describes old Lorenzo Tio as a Mexican-born teacher who used a baton.

segments.title: Old Creole songs, his brother, and Mardi Gras
segments.summary: Picou says his brother composed Creole songs; they discuss titles and translations and playing them at Mardi Gras.

segments.title: Albert-system versus Boehm clarinet and embouchure
segments.summary: Picou prefers the Albert clarinet for jazz because it has fewer keys; talk of tone and where to put the teeth.

segments.title: How bands learned tunes and brass band tunes turned to jazz
segments.summary: Interviewer asks about learning new tunes and when brass band pieces such as Didn't He Ramble were jazzed.

segments.title: How Picou learned and composed the blues
segments.summary: Picou claims to be first to compose the blues, telling how he and bassist Jimmy Brown heard a railroad work gang singing and made it into a tune in the District.

segments.title: Playing nightly in the District for tips and pay
segments.summary: After a question on marriage, Picou describes eight-to-four shifts at a dollar and a quarter, no dancing, requests, and a $50 tip.

segments.title: Food, a restaurant and walking to work
segments.summary: They talk about eating at a little restaurant, its meal, which musicians went there, and walking to jobs.

segments.title: Playing for Lula White and Tony Jackson in the mansions
segments.summary: Picou played clarinet and piano in the front parlor at Lula White's; talk of Tony Jackson's tunes, Jelly Roll Morton, hours and no shows.

segments.title: The French Opera, languages and band concerts
segments.summary: Picou loved the French Opera near his boyhood home, discusses French and Spanish, band concerts, and playing in the opera orchestra.

segments.title: Picou's clarinet pupils: Nelson, Darensbourg, Nicholas, Hall, Noone
segments.summary: Asked about pupils, Picou names Louis Nelson, Joe Darensbourg, Albert Nicholas, Edmond Hall and Jimmie Noone.

segments.title: White students and Sam Dutrey
segments.summary: Interviewer asks if white musicians studied with him and notes Achille Baquet; Dutrey is mentioned.

segments.title: Touring in a band with Bab Frank and Papa Celestin
segments.summary: Picou agrees he was in a big brass band that travelled widely.

segments.title: First trip to Chicago with Manuel Perez
segments.summary: Picou went to Chicago before World War I with Manuel Perez, working at Johnson's Cabaret and a State Street theatre.

segments.title: E-flat clarinet, mouthpieces and reeds
segments.summary: Picou talks about the E-flat clarinet in brass bands, mouthpiece alterations, and using number three reeds scraped with glass.

segments.title: Advice to young clarinet students and embouchure
segments.summary: Picou tells students to keep lips firm, and says he only ever covered the bottom teeth.

segments.title: His best pupils: Adolph Alexander and George
segments.summary: Picou names Adolph Alexander and an older pupil George, still playing on Royal Street.

segments.title: George Lewis, Albert Burbank and the song A La Ba
segments.summary: Picou says Burbank was one of his pupils and that his brother wrote the words of A La Ba.

segments.title: Bands he played in: Excelsior, Bloom, Robichaux, Moret, Independent
segments.summary: Picou runs through bands including Manuel Perez's Excelsior, Joe Bloom's orchestra, sixteen years with Robichaux, George Moret, Duconge, and his own Golden Leaf and Independent bands.

segments.title: Advice on making a clarinet part and jazzing tunes
segments.summary: Picou says they changed waltz time to jazz time and figured out clarinet parts by ear while the band played.

segments.title: Solos, piano players and the best drummers
segments.summary: Picou discusses solos in the old days, scarcity of piano players and drummers, and Louis Cottrell and others.

segments.title: Old band instruments, violins and Tiger Rag
segments.summary: They discuss absent saxophones, melophone, sousaphone, violins as lead, and Tiger Rag.

segments.title: His clarinet and its curved bell
segments.summary: Picou describes his French-made Albert-system clarinet with a curved bell.

segments.title: Learning the clarinet in eight months and when to start
segments.summary: Picou learned in eight months and says a boy should start around sixteen and when he wants to.

segments.title: Years with Papa Celestin, and pupils Arodin and Roppolo
segments.summary: Picou says he played sixteen years with Celestin, and pupils include Sidney Arodin and Roppolo.

segments.title: Sidney Bechet and learning to read music
segments.summary: Picou says Bechet learned on a tin flute, and that students should learn to read music first.

segments.title: Picou's photographs, Tony Jackson, and a visit planned
segments.summary: Picou keeps sheet music and old photographs and agrees to show them; Tony Jackson is mentioned, and the interviewer asks for a tune.

segments.title: Unrecorded compositions, including one on High Society
segments.summary: Picou has four compositions never recorded, including a high society variation, which bands found too hard.
